1.pericope_label: The sabbatical year of rest for the land

schools.summary: Gill places the speech not on the mount during the forty days but after Moses came down and the tabernacle was set up, while Israel still lay encamped about the mountain; the words may be rendered by or near Mount Sinai, and Josephus reports these laws delivered while Israel lay encamped under it.

Henry finds several reasons in the law at once: God would show them he was their landlord and they tenants at will under him, since landlords stipulate when their tenants shall break up the ground and when they shall let it rest; it was besides a kindness to the land, keeping it in heart for a posterity whose satisfaction God would have them consult; and they were brought to live in dependence upon divine providence, finding that as man lives not by bread alone, so he has bread not by his own industry alone. He closes on what the year figured, the spiritual rest believers enter through Christ, our true Noah, who gives us comfort concerning our work and the toil of our hands because of the ground the Lord hath cursed — and as the fruits of this sabbath were enjoyed in common, so the salvation wrought by Christ is a common salvation.

Clarke turns the practical objection into an argument: if it required all the annual produce of the field to support the inhabitants, how could the people be nourished in the seventh year? God sent his blessing in an especial manner on the sixth year, which brought forth fruit for three; and the miracle proves the divine authenticity of the law, for no man in his senses, without God's authority, could have made such an ordinance, since the sixth year would have amply refuted his pretensions. Wesley agrees with Gill that the particle bears the sense of near, so that there is no need to disturb the history here.

Ellicott takes the mountain for the mountainous tract rather than the peak, and thinks the chapter itself out of place: it should have followed the chapter on the festivals, since the sabbatical year and the jubilee are closely connected with those regulations, and the isolation of these ordinances can be explained only on the principle laid down by the second Temple authorities, that many sections are transposed and there is no strict sequence in the Law. From the same canons he lists what counted as cultivation — no planting of trees, cutting of dried-up branches, breaking off of withered leaves, smoking under the plants to kill insects, or besmearing unripe fruit with soil — though as much land might be worked as was needed for the taxes and for the wave sheaf and the two wave-loaves. Keil sets the institution beside the weekly one, and explains whose the produce was: what grew of itself was not to be reaped by the owner, but masters and servants, labourers and visitors, cattle and game alike were to eat of it away from the field, so that it became common to all.

positions.position: after Moses came down and the tabernacle was set up, Israel still encamped near the mountain — by or near Sinai
in the mountainous tract rather than at the peak; the chapter is transposed out of its proper place after the festivals

themes: the land shall keep a sabbath unto the LORD
six years thou shalt sow thy field
that which groweth of its own accord

8.pericope_label: The jubilee proclaimed on the day of atonement

schools.summary: Gill weighs three derivations of the name — from the peculiar sound of the trumpet; from the instrument itself, which the Jews suppose a ram's horn, jobel in Arabic signifying a ram; or, as he thinks best, from the verb to bring back, because at this time men were returned to their liberty, estates and families. Calvin calls this the most illustrious of the three sabbaths, since by it the state of the people, as to persons and houses and property alike, was renewed; its main feature, he insists, was the solemnity showing them a people separated from other nations, that being redeemed anew they might devote themselves entirely to God their Deliverer.

Henry holds for the forty-ninth year, which by a very common form of speech is called the fiftieth, referring the argument to the chronologer Calvisius and noting that seven sabbaths of weeks were reckoned from passover to pentecost, itself called the fiftieth day. He marks the day chosen for the proclamation: when they had been humbling and afflicting their souls for sin, then they were made to hear this voice of joy and gladness, and when their peace was made with God, then liberty was proclaimed — for the removal of guilt is necessary to make way for the entrance of all true comfort. In allusion to that proclamation it was foretold of our Lord Jesus that he should preach the acceptable year of the Lord.

Clarke allows either reading of the year, supposing Moses may include the preceding jubilee and so make up fifty with the forty-ninth, or that he speaks of proclaiming it on the forty-ninth and celebrating it on the fiftieth; some place it on the forty-ninth to keep it from being confounded with the sabbatical year, but he thinks the fiftieth the real jubilee. Wesley argues from usage the other way: the weekly sabbath is called the seventh day because it truly was so, being next after the six and distinct from them all; in like manner the jubilee is called the fiftieth because it comes next after seven times seven and is distinct from them all. He finds a further use in the institution, that inheritances, families and tribes might be kept entire until the Messiah came, who was to be known by the tribe and family out of which he came.

Ellicott reads the phrase as count seven weeks of years, the seven days of each week standing for so many years, and reports the second Temple reckoning that since the first sabbatical year fell in the twenty-first year after the entrance into Canaan, the first jubilee fell in the sixty-fourth. He presses the connection with the atonement to its moral: at the close of the great Day, when the Hebrew realised that his heavenly Father had annulled his sins, he was called to proclaim by nine blasts of the cornet that he too had freed every encumbered family estate — inasmuch as God has forgiven his debts, he also is to forgive his debtors. Keil looks past the etymology to what the blast recalled: the far-reaching horn had been the signal of the Lord's descent upon Sinai, and as Israel came up to the mountain at that sound, so at the expiration of the forty-nine years the same blast went through the land.

debates.question: Did the jubilee fall on the forty-ninth year or the fiftieth?

positions.position: the forty-ninth, called the fiftieth by a common form of speech, as pentecost is called the fiftieth day
the fiftieth, being next after seven times seven and distinct from them all

the trumpet of the jubile to sound on the day of atonement

11.pericope_label: The fiftieth year hallowed, and no man to oppress his brother in the sale

schools.summary: Gill takes the verse to settle the question of the year: that a jubilee shall that fiftieth year be shows it was not the forty-ninth, as many learned men have asserted, induced chiefly by the reason that two years would then come together in which there was neither sowing nor reaping; but God, who could cause the earth to bring forth fruit for three years, could make it bring forth enough for four. To make their opinion agree with this passage they must reckon the foregoing jubilee as one of the fifty and begin their account thence — which could not be done in the first account of the jubilee at all.

Clarke finds the name unsettled: Josephus says it signifies liberty, but that is rather the intention of the institution than the meaning of the term; the rabbins say a ram's horn, but no ancient version acknowledges that sense except the Chaldee; the most natural derivation is from a verb meaning to bring back or recall. He adds that this wise and excellent institution appears to have been little regarded after the Babylonish captivity, and must have ceased altogether when the Jews were brought under a foreign yoke. He reads the whole as typical of two things — of the Gospel dispensation, when all who believe are redeemed from the bondage of sin and repossess the favour and image of God, and of the general resurrection, which Parkhurst calls a lively prefiguration of the grand consummation, introduced in like manner by the trump of God. On the sale he states the ground of the prohibition sharply: he that buys an article at less than it is worth, or sells one for more, is no better than a thief. Wesley puts both sides, that neither is the seller to require more, nor the buyer to take advantage of his brother's necessities to give him less than the worth of it.

Ellicott reports the unanimous testimony of the second-Temple authorities, Philo and Josephus among them, and draws the consequence: as the forty-ninth year is the sabbatical year and the fiftieth the jubilee, there were two successive fallow years. On the sale he reports how the rule against overreaching was enforced — if anyone bought or sold a thing for a sixth part more than its value the aggrieved party might have the excess returned, and if the difference exceeded a sixth the contract could be rescinded altogether — and presses the vendor's side, that he sells not the land but a certain number of crops, so that the fallow sabbatical years falling within the term are not counted among them. Keil says the same of the pricing, that they were to sell only the produce of the yearly revenues up to the next jubilee, making the price higher or lower according to the number of years.

debates.question: Were there two successive fallow years?

positions.position: yes — the forty-ninth is the sabbatical year and the fiftieth the jubilee; God who gave fruit for three years could give it for four

themes: a jubile shall that fiftieth year be unto you
ye shall not oppress one another
according to the number of years of the fruits he shall sell unto thee

20.pericope_label: The blessing of the sixth year, and the land not to be sold for ever

schools.summary: Gill takes the objection for what it betrays: it is the speech of such as are of little faith, who disbelieve the promise and indulge an anxiety how they shall be fed in a year when there is neither tillage of land nor pruning of trees. Calvin makes more of the difficulty — men will never be obedient to God's precepts unless their distrust of him is corrected, and will always be ingenious in laying hold of pretexts for disobedience; yet here the difficulty was a specious excuse, for famine might have destroyed them in those two years, and whence were they to get seed to sow after the land had rested a whole year? Not without reason, then, does God deliver them from this doubt by promising such abundance in the sixth year as should suffice for the two following. Calvin also warns that the reason for the law of tenure was peculiar to the children of Abraham and can hardly be applied to other nations, since the land was divided by lot as though God had by his own hand located them in their stations.

Henry says that God, having a particular propriety in this land, would by the restraint keep them sensible of it; and that since they were strangers and sojourners with him there, having his tabernacle among them, to alienate their part would be in effect to cut themselves off from communion with God, of which it was the token. He finds the gospel in the office of the kinsman: he is called Goel, the redeemer, to whom belonged the right of redeeming the land, and this typified Christ, who assumed our nature that he might be our kinsman, bone of our bone, and who, being the only kinsman we have that is able to do it, has the right of redemption — for as to all our other kinsmen, their shoe must be plucked off, since they cannot redeem.

Clarke calls the objection a very natural question, which only the sovereign promise of the next verse could lay to rest; on the tenure he says they were to consider themselves merely tenants to the great landholder, and thinks the arrangement favourable to religion, since men who feel they have nothing they can call their own on earth must often be put in mind of a permanent dwelling in the heavenly inheritance. Wesley makes the three years not three complete years but in great part — the portion of the sixth year between harvest and the beginning of the seventh, the whole of the seventh, and the portion of the eighth before harvest; and this is added, he says, to show the equity of the command, for as God would hereby try their faith, so he gave an eminent proof of his own exact providence.

Ellicott counts the same three portions and draws the parallel with the manna: as at the institution of the weekly Sabbath God sent down a double portion every sixth day to make up for the day of rest, so he exercises a special providence every sixth year by blessing the soil with a treble crop; he notices that the question properly applies to the eighth year rather than the seventh, since the seventh is supplied by the harvest of the sixth. Keil states the rule of tenure in its own words: the land shall not be sold litsmithuth, literally to annihilation, that is, so as to vanish away from or be for ever lost to the seller; and the same verse lays down how a man compelled by poverty to sell his patrimony was to recover it by redemption.

themes: what shall we eat the seventh year?
I will command my blessing upon you in the sixth year
the land shall not be sold for ever: for the land is mine

24.pericope_label: The right of redemption, and the kinsman-redeemer

schools.summary: Gill draws from the wording the rule that poverty alone can justify the sale, and cites Maimonides: no man may sell his field unless his distress presses him and forces him to it, nor sell his estate to put money into his purse, or to trade with, or to purchase goods or cattle, but only for food. On the reckoning of the redemption money he sets out the arithmetic — count how many years have passed since the sale and how many remain to the jubilee, so that if just half the time is gone, half the price is repaid to the purchaser, and if the halves are unequal, then in proportion. Calvin marks how far the permission goes beyond what other nations allowed: before the jubilee came, God permits not only the relations to redeem land sold by a poor man but the seller himself, if no other redeemer interposed, whereas elsewhere the like power was given to relations with a different object, the preservation of the family name, and the seller was never allowed to redeem unless a special clause stood in the contract.

Clarke notes that the kinsman is called in the text goel, the redeemer, and asks whether this was not a lively emblem of the redemption of man by Christ Jesus: that he might have a right to redeem man he took upon him human nature and became a kinsman of the great family of the human race, thereby possessing the right of redeeming that fallen nature of which he took part. Wesley says the same in a clause, that the redeemer here was an eminent type of Christ, made near akin to us by taking our flesh that he might perform the work of redemption for us.

Ellicott draws the consequence of the tenancy — being simply tenants at will, the land is not even to remain with the purchaser until the jubilee, but the buyer is to grant the seller every opportunity of redeeming it before that time — and observes that poverty is the only reason the Law here supposes might lead a man to part with his field, from which the second-Temple authorities concluded that no one may sell his patrimony on speculation, which accounts for the horror Naboth expressed to Ahab at giving away the inheritance of his fathers. He fills out the redeemer's office from elsewhere in the Law: the word is applied to one who, by virtue of being nearest of kin, had not only to redeem the patrimony but to marry the childless widow of his brother and to avenge his blood. He closes on the design of the whole provision, to secure to each family a permanent interest in the soil and to prevent the accumulation of land in the hands of the greedy few who are ever anxious to join field unto field, precluding both landless beggars and too extensive landed proprietors — similar laws obtaining among other nations, Solon making it a law that no one should acquire as much land as he wished, while Plato held that no individual should possess more than four times the quantity held by the lowest owner. Keil states the last of the three cases: if a man had not earned as much as was required to make compensation for the recovery of his land, what he had sold was to remain with the buyer until the jubilee, and then to go out.

themes: ye shall grant a redemption for the land
if thy brother be waxen poor, and hath sold away some of his possession
then let him count the years of the sale thereof

29.pericope_label: Houses in walled cities, houses in villages, and the cities of the Levites

schools.summary: Calvin argues the exception from the nature of the two properties: a house does not supply daily food as a field does, so it is more tolerable to be without a house than without a field; but the country houses had to be excepted, being appendages to the land — what use in harvesting the fruits if you had no place to store them, and how could oxen plough without stalls in the neighbourhood? He adds a public reason for the Levites' privilege, that the provision was made not only out of favour to them but because it concerned the whole people that they should be posted like sentries in the place God had assigned them. Gill notes that no Levite had a field of his own, the suburbs belonging to them in common, which is why they might not agree together to sell it.

Clarke explains the difference put between a city house and a country one: the city house might be built for trade merely, whereas the country house was attached to the inheritance God had divided among the families, so that the same law had to apply to the house as to the inheritance. He reasons on both sides of the year of grace — the former owner might have sold rashly or under some urgent necessity, and so a year was allowed him to reconsider, while the purchaser must have been at great expense to fit the place for his work, and without some certainty of permanent possession no such purchases would ever have been made. On the Levites he anticipates the objection and turns it round: a Levite could not ultimately sell his house, and why — because Moses framed his laws so much in favour of the priesthood? Just the reverse, for they were so far from being peculiarly favoured that they had no inheritance in Israel at all, and because their houses in those cities were the whole they could call their own, these could not be ultimately alienated. Wesley gives the reasons why city houses were not to revert: no confusion of tribes could follow their alienation; the seller had a greater propriety in a house than in land, it being commonly built by his own cost and diligence; and God would hereby encourage men to possess houses in such places, since fulness of inhabitants in cities was a great strength to the whole land.

Ellicott grounds the distinction higher up: houses in walled cities are not the creation of God allotted by his command to the tribes, but the work of man, who builds them up and razes them at his own will, so that the law of jubilee does not apply to these temporary buildings. He suspects the text itself at the Levites' clause, thinking it more than probable that a negative particle has dropped out and that it originally stood, and if one of the Levites doth not redeem it — the Vulgate still has the negative. Keil says the meadows were not saleable, nor even to be let until the jubilee, because if sold the Levites would have nothing left to feed their cattle upon.

debates.question: Has the text of the Levites' clause been corrupted?

positions.position: yes — a negative particle has probably dropped out; it should read, if one of the Levites doth not redeem it, and the Vulgate still has the negative

themes: within a full year may he redeem it
the houses of the villages shall be counted as the fields
the field of the suburbs of their cities may not be sold

35.pericope_label: The poor brother to be relieved, and no usury taken of him

schools.summary: Gill adds that the relief was not to stop at present necessity, but that money was to be lent to put the man in a way of business and get his living for the future, without requiring any interest for it; and on the prohibition he says the text speaks only of persons in poor and necessitous circumstances.

Henry sets the duty in the plainest terms: poverty and decay are great grievances, and very common, for the poor we have always with us; and the relief commanded is of three kinds — by sympathy, in pitying the poor; by service, in doing for them; and by supply, in giving to them according to their necessity and our ability. He notes the argument the law itself uses against extortion, fear thy God, and the reason annexed, that they may live with thee, for they may yet be serviceable to thee: the rich can as ill spare the poor as the poor can spare the rich, and it becomes those that have received mercy to show mercy.

Clarke observes that usury at present signifies unlawful interest for money, though properly it means the reward or compensation given for the use of a thing, and is principally spoken of money. Wesley states the prohibition broadly, that all kinds of usury are in this case forbidden, whether of money or of victuals or of anything commonly lent upon condition of receiving it back with advantage and overplus; and he adds the limit of the case — if a man borrow in his necessity there can be no doubt this law is binding still, but it cannot be thought to bind where money is borrowed for the purchase of lands, for trade, or for other improvements, since there it is reasonable that the lender should share with the borrower in the profit. He narrows the other term too, taking the sojourner here to mean proselytes only, since of other strangers they were permitted to take usury.

Keil and Ellicott both press the literal force of the phrase: the Hebrew is that his hand wavers or trembles beside thee, meaning that he is no longer able to sustain himself alone, and the command that follows is literally to lay hold of him — thou shalt take him by the arm to help him out of his misfortune. Ellicott corrects the rendering of the next clause as well: it is not though he be a stranger or a sojourner, but as a stranger and a sojourner, the impoverished Israelite not to be treated as an outcast because want has compelled him to part with his land, but to receive the same consideration that strangers and sojourners receive, who like him hold no landed property of their own. He reports the second-Temple definitions distinguishing the two forbidden charges: if a man lends a shekel worth four denarii and receives five in return, that is usury, a charge upon money, whereas increase falls upon products, as when a dealer who has contracted to deliver wheat at twenty-five denarii takes it back at thirty and undertakes to give wine for it, though he has no wine at the time and may yet lose by the rise in wine.

debates.question: Does the prohibition of usury bind still?

positions.position: it binds where a man borrows in his necessity, but not where money is borrowed for lands, trade or improvements, since there the lender may share the profit
the text speaks only of persons in poor and necessitous circumstances

themes: if thy brother be waxen poor, then thou shalt relieve him
take thou no usury of him, or increase
fear thy God, that thy brother may live with thee

39.pericope_label: The Hebrew bondman to serve as a hired servant and go out at the jubilee

schools.summary: Gill observes that the word used for rigour is the very one used of the Egyptians when they made Israel to serve, and seems designed to put them in mind of it, that they might abstain from usage towards their brethren which they had met with from their cruellest enemies. Calvin raises the difficulty of the two terms: since liberty had already been granted the Hebrew servant in the seventh year, why is it here postponed to the fiftieth? Some answer that if the jubilee fell within the six years he must then be set free though the term were not complete, but Calvin thinks that too forced, and the view which most approves itself to him is that moderation is here specially prescribed towards those slaves who stood most exposed to violence — men would not have dared to oppress at pleasure servants soon to be free, but those who by having their ears bored had subjected themselves to the longer period would have been the more outrageously harassed had God not interposed; and this is confirmed by the command that the children should be set free along with their fathers, which did not take place in the seventh year.

Henry states the principle the law rests on: a native Israelite was never to be made a bondman for perpetuity, and if he sold himself through extreme poverty to one of his own nation, it was not to be looked upon that the master had as absolute a property in him as in a captive taken in war; he shall serve as a hired servant, of whom the master has the use only and not a despotic power. The reason given is that they are my servants — God does not make his servants slaves, and therefore their brethren must not. He turns the prohibition of rigour upon the masters: both the servant's work and his usage must be such as befit a son of Abraham, and masters who are always hectoring and domineering, unreasonable in exacting work and in giving rebukes, forget that their own Master is in heaven. He closes on the release itself, which typified our redemption from the service of sin by the grace of God in Christ, whose truth makes us free, and reports from the Jewish writers that the servants to be discharged expressed their joy for ten days before the trumpet sounded by feasting and wearing garlands on their heads, whence it is called the joyful sound.

Clarke asks what rigorous service is and answers first from the Jews, service which is not determined and service whereof there is no need; but much more is implied — labour beyond a man's strength, or too long continued, or in unhealthy places, or without sufficient food, is labour exacted with rigour and consequently inhuman, and this law is made not for the Mosaic dispensation only but for every people under heaven. Wesley presses the same clause: though thou fear not those who are in thy power and unable to right themselves, yet fear that God who has commanded thee to use them kindly, and who will avenge their cause if thou oppress them.

Ellicott adds what the second-Temple authorities counted degrading work for an Israelite bondman: he must not attend his master at the bath, nor undo the latchets of his sandals. Keil marks the line the law draws — servants bought of foreign nations might be left as an inheritance to a man's children and slave-labour performed through them, but never through his brethren the children of Israel.

debates.question: Why is the release put at the jubilee when the seventh year already freed him?

positions.position: if the jubilee fell within the six years he was freed then, though the term were incomplete
the jubilee clause protects those who by having their ears bored took the longer term and so stood most exposed to violence; hence the children go free with their fathers

themes: thou shalt not compel him to serve as a bondservant
thou shalt not rule over him with rigour, but shalt fear thy God
for they are my servants, which I brought forth out of the land of Egypt

44.pericope_label: Bondmen of the heathen, and the Israelite sold to a stranger redeemed

schools.summary: Gill reads the permission as an answer to an objection: since the Law forbids holding a brother as a bondman or putting him to the menial work of slaves, the Hebrews might fairly ask, as Jarchi puts it, who then shall I have to minister to me? Calvin observes that what God here permits as regards strangers was everywhere customary among the Gentiles, that a master's power over his slaves should last not merely until his death but pass in perpetual succession to his children; the point to notice is the antithesis, that ye shall make use of their service but over his brother no man shall rule with rigour — not that a cruel exercise of power over strangers was allowed, but that God would have the race of Abraham, whose liberator he was, exempted by certain privileges from the common lot. He sets out the redemption and its arithmetic, a power of redeeming being granted to the man's relatives or, if he had earned his price, to himself, and observes that God so mitigates his law as to lay no unjust burden on sojourners, conceding more to them than to the natives, since a man who sold himself to his brethren went out free in the seventh year while his slavery under a sojourner extended to the fiftieth; the object of the whole was that none whom God had adopted should be alienated from their race and so depart from his worship.

Clarke calls the rule of redemption equitable to sojourner and Israelite alike: they were to reckon the years he must otherwise have served until the jubilee, take the current yearly wages of a servant, and multiply the remaining years by that sum, the aggregate being the price of his redemption. Wesley gives the ground of it in a clause — the allowance is proportioned to what is given a hired servant for the like term, because it is not properly the man's person but his work and labour that was sold.

Ellicott adds the limits on the permission, that the Israelites were restricted to the Ammonites, Moabites, Edomites and Syrians who were their neighbours, and forbidden to buy any slaves at all from the seven nations in their midst whom they were ordered to destroy; and he reports how far even that permission was narrowed in practice, the second-Temple authorities enacting that the master's right over this kind of bondman is restricted to their labour, that he may not barter with them, misuse them or put them to shame, and that if he maimed one he must set him free. In contrast the Hebrew bondmen are called brethren, co-religionists in temporary servitude who are nevertheless fellow-heirs with their masters in the land — whence the same authorities enacted that there must be no difference between the daily food, raiment and dwelling of the master and of his Hebrew slave. Of the stranger who might hold such a servant he notes that he had submitted only to the seven commandments given to Noah and had not joined the Jewish religion, which is why the Chaldee renders it, if the hand of an uncircumcised sojourner wax strong. Keil marks the difference the case turns on: the servitude of an Israelite to a settler who had come to the possession of property, or to a non-Israelite dwelling in the land, was redeemable at any time.

themes: of them shall ye buy bondmen and bondmaids
over your brethren ye shall not rule one over another with rigour
after that he is sold he may be redeemed again

51.pericope_label: The price of redemption reckoned, and the year of jubilee closing all

schools.summary: Gill finishes the arithmetic: if fewer years remain to the jubilee than the man has already served, the less is given for his redemption, so that where he has served fifteen and five remain, the price falls accordingly. On the next clause he notes that the Targum of Jonathan supplies the sense our version follows, in any of the years between the sale and the jubilee, and that Aben Ezra reads so; but others take the words to mean by these — that is, by the persons already named — since the word years is not in the text at all, and the Vulgate, the Septuagint and the Oriental versions render it by these means or persons. He reads the closing verse of Christ, that those redeemed by his blood should not be perpetual servants to men, observing from the Targum of Jonathan's servants to my law that those redeemed by Christ are servants to his gospel.

Clarke closes on the ends the institution served, reporting Calmet's summary: the motive of the law was to prevent the rich from oppressing the poor and reducing them to perpetual slavery; that they should not get possession of all the lands by purchase, mortgage, or at last usurpation; that debts should not be multiplied too much, lest the poor be entirely ruined; and that slaves should not continue always, they and their wives and children, in servitude. On the closing words he marks how far the gospel goes beyond them: the Israelites were a typical people, representing those who are children of God by faith in Christ Jesus, but these last have a peculiarity of blessing, for they are not merely servants but sons — to which the apostle alludes in writing that thou art no more a servant but a son, and if a son then an heir of God through Christ. Wesley states the Israelite's duty toward a cruel Gentile master in a sentence: thou shalt not suffer it to be done, but whether magistrate or private person shalt take care according to thy capacity to get it remedied.

Ellicott presses the clause in thine eyes: as long as the man is in service his master must not treat him as a slave but behave to him as to one who hires out his labour from year to year and will after a short time be his own master again; and by in thy sight the Israelite is admonished not to be a tacit spectator of a Gentile owner's cruel treatment of his brother — though he is not to resent it in the way the Lawgiver himself once resented such a thing in Egypt, he is still to remonstrate with the cruel master and to invoke the protection of the powers that be. He decides the disputed clause without hesitation, better, if he be not redeemed by these, namely by the relations or the means indicated just above, and adds the point of the whole provision, that the heathen master is to submit to the laws of jubilee as much as the Hebrew. Keil describes the condition the man was kept in meanwhile, the buyer to hold him as a labourer engaged by the year, not ruling over him with severe oppression; and he sums up what the year accomplished — it helped every Israelite who had fallen into poverty and slavery to the recovery both of his property and of his personal freedom, so that the whole community was restored to the original condition appointed for it by God, and yet that restoration of the theocratic state was not the highest object of the year, since the observance of sabbatical rest throughout the whole land formed part of the liberty it proclaimed.

debates.question: Should the clause read in these years or by these?

positions.position: by these — by the relations or the means indicated above; the word years is not in the text, and the Vulgate, Septuagint and Oriental versions render it so
in these years — in any of the years between the sale and the jubilee, as the Targum of Jonathan and Aben Ezra

themes: according unto the number of years shall he give again the price of his redemption
he shall not rule with rigour over him in thy sight
for unto me the children of Israel are servants
